competencies.text: Describe volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, tsunamis. Describe slow processes: soil erosion, saltwater intrusion.

days.title: Geologic Processes — Fast & Slow
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

By the end of today's lesson, you will be able to describe fast geologic processes (volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, tsunamis) and slow geologic processes (soil erosion, saltwater intrusion), and explain their causes and effects.

⏱️ Fast vs. Slow Geologic Processes

CategoryTime ScaleExamples
Fast (catastrophic)Seconds to daysVolcanic eruptions, earthquakes, tsunamis, landslides
Slow (gradual)Years to centuriesSoil erosion, saltwater intrusion, weathering, subsidence

🌋 Volcanic Eruptions

A volcano is an opening in Earth's crust where magma, gases, and ash escape from the mantle. Eruptions occur when pressure from dissolved gases builds up inside the magma chamber.

Type of EruptionCharacteristicsExample
EffusiveGentle lava flow, low gas contentHawaiian volcanoes, Mayon's calmer phases
ExplosiveViolent blast of ash, gas, pyroclastic flowsPinatubo 1991, Taal 2020, Mayon 2018

Hazards: Lava flows, pyroclastic flows, ashfall, volcanic gases, lahars (mudflows), tsunami (if eruption is near or under the sea).

🌎 Earthquakes

An earthquake is a sudden release of energy in Earth's crust, usually caused by movement along faults (tectonic or volcanic).

TermDefinition
Focus (hypocenter)Point inside Earth where the earthquake begins
EpicenterPoint directly above the focus on the surface
MagnitudeMeasure of energy released (e.g., Richter, Moment Magnitude scale)
IntensityMeasure of shaking and damage at a specific location (e.g., PEIS)
AftershocksSmaller quakes that follow the main shock

Hazards: Ground shaking, ground rupture, landslides, liquefaction, tsunamis, fires, and building collapse.

🌊 Tsunamis

A tsunami is a series of large ocean waves usually caused by:

  • Underwater earthquakes (most common — especially along subduction zones)
  • Volcanic eruptions (like the 1883 Krakatoa eruption)
  • Landslides into the ocean
  • Meteorite impacts (rare)

Warning signs: Strong shaking, sudden withdrawal of the sea (water recedes), loud roar.

Philippine example: The 1976 Moro Gulf tsunami killed over 5,000 people — the deadliest in PH history.

🌱 Soil Erosion — A Slow Process

Soil erosion is the gradual removal of topsoil by wind, water, or human activity.

CauseEffect
DeforestationLoss of root systems that hold soil together
OvergrazingCompacted, exposed soil washes away
Improper farmingErosion on hillsides without terracing
Heavy rain & floodsRapid washing away of topsoil
Strong windsBlowing away dry topsoil

Effects: Reduced soil fertility, lower crop yields, sedimentation in rivers, landslides, and desertification.

Prevention: Contour plowing, terracing, cover crops, reforestation, and agroforestry.

🌊 Saltwater Intrusion — A Slow Process

Saltwater intrusion is the movement of saline water into freshwater aquifers, usually caused by:

  • Over-pumping of groundwater near the coast
  • Rising sea levels (climate change)
  • Droughts reducing freshwater recharge
  • Human-made channels allowing seawater inland

Effects:

  • Wells become salty — unusable for drinking
  • Farmland becomes saline — crops fail
  • Freshwater ecosystems disrupted
  • Coastal communities lose access to clean water

Prevention: Managed aquifer recharge, desalination (as a last resort), reducing groundwater pumping, and protecting coastal wetlands/mangroves.

🇵🇭 Philippine Context

  • The Philippines is highly vulnerable to all of these — being in the Ring of Fire AND typhoon belt.
  • PHIVOLCS (Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology) monitors volcanoes, earthquakes, and tsunami threats.
  • PHIVOLCS uses a hazard warning system with alert levels (Level 0 to 5 for volcanoes).

📌 Quick Check

  • What causes a tsunami? (Answer: usually an underwater earthquake; also volcanic eruptions and landslides)
  • What is soil erosion, and what causes it? (Answer: gradual removal of topsoil by wind, water, or human activity — often caused by deforestation)
  • What causes saltwater intrusion? (Answer: over-pumping of groundwater, rising sea levels, and droughts)

days.title: Match Game — Geologic Hazards
days.content:
🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each geologic process or concept to its correct description. There are 8 pairs and unlimited retakes to reach 75%.

match.right: Escape of magma, ash, and gases through an opening in Earth's crust
Gentle lava flow with low gas content — like Hawaiian volcanoes
Violent blast with ash, gas, and pyroclastic flows — like Pinatubo 1991
Point on Earth's surface directly above the earthquake focus
Series of large ocean waves usually caused by underwater earthquakes
Gradual removal of topsoil by wind, water, or human activity
Seawater seeping into freshwater aquifers — often from over-pumping
Agency that monitors Philippine volcanoes, earthquakes, and tsunamis

days.title: Scenario Challenge — Volcanoes & Earthquakes
days.content:
🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Read each scenario and choose the best reasoning. There are 5 scenarios. You have unlimited retakes to reach 75%.

scenario.text: 🌋 Taal Volcano erupts, and PHIVOLCS raises the alert level to 4. What does this mean for residents nearby?

choices.label: A) A hazardous explosive eruption is imminent — they must evacuate immediately
C) Nothing — alert levels are only for scientists
D) It means the volcano is safe to visit

scenario.text: 🌊 You're at the beach and the water suddenly recedes far out to sea, exposing the ocean floor. What should you do?

choices.label: A) Run to higher ground immediately — a tsunami is coming
B) Walk out to explore the exposed ocean floor
C) Take photos to post online
D) Stay in place and wait

scenario.text: 🌧️ After heavy rains, a hillside in your barangay starts to slide into the river. Which slow process likely made the hillside vulnerable?

choices.label: A) Soil erosion caused by deforestation and loss of vegetation roots

scenario.text: 🌊 A coastal barangay's wells are becoming salty, and residents can no longer use them for drinking. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: A) Saltwater intrusion from over-pumping of groundwater and rising sea levels
B) Residents added too much salt to the well
D) The wells are too deep

scenario.text: 🏠 An earthquake of magnitude 7.2 hits your province. What should you do DURING the shaking?

choices.label: A) Drop, cover, and hold — get under a sturdy table and protect your head
C) Stand in a doorway only

days.title: Formative Check — Escape the Geohazard Lab
days.content:
🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Geohazard Lab

You have 3 lives and 6 keys to unlock. You need 75% (5 of 6) to pass. Take your time — read every option carefully.

escape.text: What is a tsunami usually caused by?
What is the point on Earth's surface directly above an earthquake's origin called?
Which of the following is a SLOW geologic process?

choices.label: A) The gradual removal of topsoil by wind, water, or human activity
C) The formation of new soil

escape.text: Which agency monitors volcanic and seismic activity in the Philippines?
What is the BEST response during a strong earthquake?

choices.label: A) Drop, cover, and hold under a sturdy table
C) Take an elevator to the ground floor
